body:
The emergence of a new phase of the freedom struggle

The Civil Disobedience Movement of 1930–1934 was a major phase of India's struggle against British colonial rule. Led by Mahatma Gandhi and the Indian National Congress, it sought to challenge British authority through organised, largely non-violent resistance. Its immediate symbol was the deliberate violation of the British salt law at Dandi in Gujarat on 6 April 1930.

The movement developed from political changes during the 1920s. The Non-Cooperation Movement of 1920–1922 had encouraged Indians to withdraw support from British institutions. However, Gandhi suspended it in February 1922 after protesters attacked a police station at Chauri Chaura in the United Provinces, killing 22 policemen. Gandhi believed that a mass struggle claiming to follow non-violence could not continue without greater discipline.

After its withdrawal, Congress leaders differed over their next method. C. R. Das and Motilal Nehru helped establish the Swaraj Party in 1923 to enter legislative councils and oppose colonial policies from within. Gandhi's supporters continued constructive activities such as promoting khadi, village work and social reform. These activities also helped maintain contact with people outside the major cities.

Political developments during 1928–1929

Opposition to the Simon Commission

The British government appointed the Simon Commission in 1927 to review India's constitutional arrangements. When the commission arrived in India in 1928, it faced widespread protests because all its members were British and it contained no Indian representative. Demonstrators raised the slogan Simon Go Back.

The protests strengthened demands that Indians should determine their own political future. In October 1929, Viceroy Lord Irwin announced the possibility of dominion status at an unspecified future date and proposed discussions about constitutional reform. Dominion status meant substantial self-government while retaining a constitutional connection with the British Crown. The absence of a definite commitment disappointed nationalists demanding complete independence.

Economic distress

The agricultural depression added to political dissatisfaction. Falling agricultural prices, especially during the worldwide economic crisis beginning in 1929, reduced the income of peasants who sold commercial crops. Their difficulty in paying land revenue increased resentment against colonial revenue demands. These economic grievances later influenced peasant participation in civil disobedience.

Gujarat had already witnessed the Bardoli Satyagraha of 1928, led by Vallabhbhai Patel against an increase in land revenue. Bardoli was an earlier, separate struggle; it demonstrated the importance of organised rural resistance before the national campaign of 1930.

The Lahore Congress and Purna Swaraj

At its Lahore session in December 1929, the Indian National Congress, under the presidency of Jawaharlal Nehru, adopted Purna Swaraj, meaning complete independence, as its objective.

The Congress declared that 26 January 1930 would be observed as Independence Day. People were asked to take a pledge supporting the struggle for complete independence. This was a declaration of political purpose, not the actual end of British rule.

Gandhi now needed an issue that would make the demand for independence understandable in everyday life. He chose the salt tax and prepared to begin the Salt March from Sabarmati Ashram on 12 March 1930.

Meaning of civil disobedience

Civil disobedience is the deliberate and open violation of a law considered unjust, as a form of political protest. In Gandhi's method of satyagraha, such resistance was to remain non-violent, disciplined and truthful, even when protesters faced arrest or punishment.

Prelims focus

  • February 1922: Non-Cooperation Movement withdrawn following the Chauri Chaura incident.
  • 1928: Simon Commission faced protests because it had no Indian member.
  • 1928: Vallabhbhai Patel led the Bardoli Satyagraha in Gujarat.
  • December 1929: Lahore Congress, presided over by Jawaharlal Nehru, adopted Purna Swaraj.
  • 26 January 1930: Independence Day pledge was observed.
  • Trap: The 1930 declaration of Purna Swaraj did not mean that India became independent in 1930.

[NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, 'Nationalism in India', printed pp. 62–63; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 'The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947', printed pp. 119–121; IGNOU, Indian National Movement, Unit 15, 'Civil Disobedience Movement', sections 15.2–15.3; Rajghat Samadhi Committee, Government of India, 'Life Events of Mahatma Gandhi', entries for 1922–1930, accessed 21 November 2026.]

title: Background: From Non-Cooperation to Civil Disobedience

body:
The salt tax and government monopoly

Under British colonial rule, the government controlled the production and sale of salt and imposed a tax on it. The salt monopoly restricted the ability of Indians to produce and distribute salt independently, while the salt tax increased the burden associated with obtaining an essential food item.

Salt was necessary for everyone, irrespective of income, occupation, caste or religion. A wealthy merchant, a factory worker and a poor agricultural labourer all needed it. Consequently, Gandhi believed that opposition to the salt law could express a grievance shared by people who otherwise had different economic interests.

The salt tax was especially suitable for a mass campaign because it connected a simple daily necessity with a much larger political issue: the authority of a foreign government to control Indian resources and impose laws on Indians.

Central idea: Gandhi selected salt because a common daily necessity could make the wider demand for freedom understandable to ordinary people and unite different sections of society.

The 11 demands presented to Lord Irwin

Before launching the movement, Gandhi presented 11 demands to Viceroy Lord Irwin at the end of January 1930. The demands addressed different grievances rather than salt alone. They were intended to provide a common basis for support among peasants, industrialists and other sections of Indian society.

Important demands included:

  • Abolition of the salt tax and government salt monopoly.
  • Reduction of the land revenue burden on cultivators.
  • Reduction of military expenditure and high salaries paid to senior officials.
  • Protection for Indian textile industries against foreign competition.
  • Prohibition of intoxicating liquor.
  • Release of political prisoners.

The demands were presented as immediate measures that the government could take. They did not replace the Congress's broader objective of Purna Swaraj.

From demands to a planned breach of law

On 2 March 1930, Gandhi wrote a further letter to Lord Irwin explaining why he intended to violate the salt law. The government was given an opportunity to respond before the planned campaign. Gandhi had indicated that if the demands were not met by 11 March 1930, civil disobedience would follow.

Irwin did not accept the demands. Gandhi therefore proceeded with the planned march from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi, a village on the Gujarat coast.

Why salt was an effective strategy

A simple action with a wider meaning

Breaking the salt law did not require control of a legislature or possession of expensive equipment. At a suitable coastal location, people could collect natural salt or produce it by evaporating seawater. Doing so without government permission directly challenged the colonial salt regulations.

Publicly violating the law would demonstrate that Indians were no longer willing to treat every colonial regulation as legitimate merely because the government had enacted it. A local act could therefore become a national political statement.

A common issue did not erase other grievances

Salt was the starting point, not the only issue in the movement. Peasants remained concerned about land revenue, industrialists about trade restrictions, workers about wages and working conditions, and many communities about their civil and political rights. As the campaign developed, these concerns influenced the forms of protest adopted in different places.

Prelims focus

  • Lord Irwin: Viceroy to whom Gandhi presented the demands before the Salt March.
  • 11: Number of demands put forward by Gandhi.
  • 2 March 1930: Gandhi's detailed letter explaining his intention to break the salt law.
  • 11 March 1930: Deadline associated with the proposed campaign.
  • Salt strategy: Opposition to the tax and government monopoly on an essential commodity.
  • Trap: The Salt March was not a movement concerned only with the price of salt; it challenged colonial political authority.

[NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, 'Nationalism in India', printed pp. 63–64; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 'The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947', printed p. 121; Gandhi Heritage Portal, 'Background to the Salt Satyagraha', entries for January–March 1930, including Gandhi's letter of 2 March, accessed 21 November 2026; IGNOU, Indian National Movement, Unit 15, section 15.3, 'The Lahore Session'.]

title: Why Gandhi Chose Salt as the Basis of the Movement

body:
The march begins at Sabarmati Ashram

On 12 March 1930, Mahatma Gandhi left Sabarmati Ashram in Ahmedabad, Gujarat, accompanied by 78 selected volunteers. Gandhi was in addition to these 78 companions. As the march proceeded, many more people joined or gathered to support the procession.

The march was also called the Salt March or Dandi March. It covered more than 240 miles, approximately 390 km, and passed through numerous villages and towns in Gujarat. The journey is commonly described as a 24-day march, with halts along the way.

Gandhi addressed gatherings during the journey. He explained the meaning of swaraj, criticised colonial laws and urged participants to maintain non-violence. The march therefore served two purposes: it carried Gandhi towards the coast and mobilised public support along the route.

Important places and dates along the route

  • 12 March: Departure from Sabarmati Ashram, Ahmedabad.
  • 15 March: Nadiad.
  • 16 March: Anand.
  • 18 March: Borsad.
  • 19–20 March: Passage through the Ras area and crossing of the Mahi River.
  • 26 March: Bharuch, historically called Broach; the march crossed the Narmada River and continued towards Ankleshwar.
  • 1 April: Surat; the march crossed the Tapi, also called the Tapti, and Gandhi addressed a mass meeting in Surat.
  • 3 April: Navsari.
  • 5 April: Arrival at Dandi.

This sequence explains why Gujarat occupies a central place in the history of the movement. Ahmedabad was the starting point, several towns of central and southern Gujarat hosted the marchers, and Dandi on the Arabian Sea coast became the site of the decisive breach of the salt law.

Vallabhbhai Patel and the preparations

Vallabhbhai Patel helped mobilise support in Gujarat before the march. While addressing a meeting in Ras village, near Borsad, he was arrested on 7 March 1930, five days before Gandhi's departure.

His arrest provoked protests and strengthened public attention around the planned campaign. Patel's role was important in organising rural support, but he was not the person who led the Salt March from Sabarmati to Dandi. Gandhi led that march.

The salt law is broken on 6 April 1930

The marchers arrived at Dandi on 5 April 1930. The following morning, 6 April 1930, Gandhi deliberately broke the British salt law by collecting natural salt from the seashore. The making of salt through the evaporation of seawater also became a method of defiance.

Dandi is a coastal village in present-day Navsari district, Gujarat. Its importance in the national movement arises from the fact that a simple action there marked the opening of a widespread campaign of civil disobedience.

Arrival and action are different dates: Gandhi reached Dandi on 5 April 1930, but the historic violation of the salt law took place on 6 April 1930.

How the march became a national event

The procession began with a small, disciplined group but attracted crowds at its halts. News of the march spread beyond Gujarat. Gandhi's example encouraged others to break salt regulations and organise related campaigns in different provinces.

The march itself was not a journey through every part of India. Its national importance came from the wider participation and protests that followed the act at Dandi.

Prelims focus

  • Starting point: Sabarmati Ashram, Ahmedabad.
  • Starting date: 12 March 1930.
  • Original companions: 78 volunteers accompanying Gandhi.
  • Distance: More than 240 miles, approximately 390 km.
  • Destination: Dandi, now in Navsari district, Gujarat.
  • Trap: Arrival at Dandi was on 5 April; the salt law was broken on 6 April 1930.
